claim: Seven infant marmosets (three females) from three different parental pairs were used as subjects in this study.
source: The subjects used in this study were seven (three females) infant common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) from three different parental pairs (two sets of twins and one set of triplets,<2 months old).
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the study subjects.

claim: Infant marmosets were observed across approximately 30 sessions during their first two months of postnatal life.
source: During their first two months of postnatal life, we measured infant marmoset behavior in a controlled context for 10 minutes approximately every 2 days.
evidence: Direct statement describing the experimental design and data collection schedule.

claim: A total of 220 observation sessions were conducted across all subjects.
source: We recorded the behaviors of each subject across ~30 sessions (28–33 per subject for a total of 220 sessions).
evidence: Direct statement providing the total number of observation sessions.

claim: Cries are immature contact calls with short duration and noisy spectral properties (high Wiener entropy).
source: As described previously (Takahashi et al., 2015), cries are immature contact calls that have a short duration and noisy spectral properties (i.e., high Wiener entropy)
evidence: Definition supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phees are mature-sounding contact calls with longer duration and tonal spectral properties (low Wiener entropy).
source: phees are mature-sounding contact calls that have a longer duration and tonal spectral properties (i.e., low Wiener entropy).
evidence: Definition provided in the text describing vocal behavior types.

claim: Cries transform into phees over the course of development.
source: Cries transform into phees over the course of development (Takahashi et al., 2015; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016; Takahashi et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The proportion of time producing cries decreased across development.
source: the proportion of time producing cries decreased across development
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Table 1) and visualization (Figure 2A).

claim: The proportion of time producing phees increased across development.
source: the proportion of time producing phees increased (Figure 2A; Table 1; Appendix 1.1)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing developmental trajectory.

claim: The proportion of postural time engaged in righting reflexes decreased across development.
source: The proportion of postural time engaged in righting reflexes decreased across development
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Table 1) and visualization (Figure 2A).

claim: The proportion of postural time engaged in hindlimb support increased across development.
source: the proportion of postural time engaged in hindlimb support increased (Figure 2A; Table 1; Appendix 1.2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing developmental trajectory.

claim: The proportion of locomotor time engaged in crawling decreased across development.
source: The proportion of locomotor time engaged in crawling decreased across development
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Table 1) and visualization (Figure 2A).

claim: The proportion of locomotor time engaged in walking increased across development.
source: the proportion of locomotor time engaged in walking increased (Figure 2A; Table 1; Appendix 1.3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and figure showing developmental trajectory.

claim: Contact calls transitioned to a more mature form around postnatal day 10.
source: contact calls transitioned to a more mature form around 10 postnatal days
evidence: Derived from analysis of maturity indices shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Postural behavior transitioned to more mature forms around postnatal day 19.
source: postural and locomotor behavior transitioned around postnatal days 19 and 21, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: Derived from analysis of maturity indices shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Locomotor behavior transitioned to more mature forms around postnatal day 21.
source: postural and locomotor behavior transitioned around postnatal days 19 and 21, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: Derived from analysis of maturity indices shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Vocal maturity indices were larger than postural maturity indices.
source: The same model showed that the vocal maturity indices were larger than the maturity indices of postural (β ±SE = −2.03±0.58, z = 3.48, p=0.0005; Appendix 1.4)
evidence: Statistical comparison using generalized linear mixed model.

claim: Vocal maturity indices were larger than locomotor maturity indices.
source: The same model showed that the vocal maturity indices were larger than the maturity indices of postural (β ±SE = −2.03±0.58, z = 3.48, p=0.0005; Appendix 1.4) and locomotor behavior (β ±SE = −2.86±0.98, z = 2.93, p=0.0034; Appendix 1.4) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison using generalized linear mixed model.

claim: Vocal development occurred earlier than postural and locomotor development.
source: In other words, vocal development occurred earlier than postural and locomotor development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from statistical analysis of maturity indices.

claim: Call duration was negatively associated with locomotor activity.
source: Call duration was negatively associated with locomotor activity (n = 9609 calls, β ±SE = −0.56±0.13, t = 4.25, Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p=0.0001; Appendix 1.5)
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear mixed effect models.

claim: Wiener entropy was positively associated with locomotor activity.
source: while Wiener entropy (higher entropy means noisier) was positively associated with locomotor activity (n = 9606 calls, β ±SE = 0.93±0.12, t = 7.68, Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p<0.0001; Appendix 1.6).
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear mixed effect models.

claim: Infant marmosets produced short, noisier calls when locomotor activity was high.
source: In other words, on average, infant marmosets produced short, noisier calls when locomotor activity was high
evidence: Interpretation of statistical results on call acoustics and locomotor activity.

claim: Infant marmosets produced longer, more tonal adult-like calls when locomotor activity was reduced.
source: and longer, more tonal adult-like calls when locomotor activity was reduced.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical results on call acoustics and locomotor activity.

claim: Locomotor activity started to increase approximately 5 seconds before immature call onsets.
source: We found that locomotor activity started to increase above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test ~5 s before the immature call onsets
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3C with bootstrap significance testing.

claim: Locomotor activity decreased back to baseline approximately 10 seconds after immature call offsets.
source: and then decrease back to inside the 95% threshold ~10 s after call offsets.
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3C with bootstrap significance testing.

claim: Locomotor activity started to decrease approximately 8 seconds before mature contact call onsets.
source: In contrast, locomotor activity started to decrease below the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test ~8 s before mature contact call onsets
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3C with bootstrap significance testing.

claim: Locomotor activity increased back to baseline approximately 10 seconds after mature contact call offsets.
source: and then increase back to inside the 95% threshold ~10 s after call offsets.
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3C with bootstrap significance testing.

claim: Average locomotor activity was higher during immature contact calls compared to mature contact calls.
source: A LMM confirmed that the average locomotor activity was higher during immature contact calls as compared to mature contact calls (n = 9609 calls, β ±SE = −0.07±0.01, t = 5.19, p<0.0001; Appendix 1.7).
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear mixed model.

claim: Locomotor activity during mature contact calls was higher during late development (PND 52-61) compared to early development (PND 1-10).
source: Locomotor activity during mature contact calls was higher during late development (PND 52–61) as compared to early development (PND 1–10) (Early = 914 calls; Late = 932 calls; β ±SE = 0.04±0.01, t = 3.05, p=0.0056; Appendix 1.8).
evidence: Statistical comparison between early and late developmental periods.

claim: Marmosets produced immature contact calls when heart rate percentiles dropped below the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test.
source: A summary of the real-time dynamics of heart rate fluctuations in the 10 s before to 10 s after vocal production revealed that marmosets produced immature contact calls when heart rate percentiles dropped below the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test (Figure 4A).
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics with bootstrap significance testing shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Production of mature contact calls occurred when heart rate percentiles went above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test.
source: Production of mature contact calls, on the other hand, occurred when heart rate percentiles went above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test.
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics with bootstrap significance testing shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Changes in arousal levels occurred at least 10 seconds before the start of the call.
source: In both cases, changes in arousal levels were 'global', meaning that the change in arousal occurred well before (at least 10 s) the start of the call.
evidence: Observation from temporal dynamics analysis of heart rate around vocal production.

claim: Heart rate percentiles were higher during mature contact calls than during immature contact calls.
source: A LMM confirmed that heart rate percentiles were higher during mature contact calls than during immature contact calls (n = 6215 calls, β ±SE = 3.38±1.45, t = 2.32, p=0.0276; Appendix 1.9).
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear mixed model.

claim: Heart rates during immature contact calls started to decrease below the 95% threshold around two weeks of age.
source: Early in postnatal life, heart rate percentiles during immature contact calls were inside the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test, but at around two weeks, heart rates during immature contact calls started to decrease below the 95% threshold.
evidence: Developmental dynamics analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mature contact calls were produced when heart rate percentiles were at or above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test during the first two months of postnatal life.
source: In contrast, mature contact calls were produced when heart rate percentiles were at, or above, the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test during the first two months of postnatal life.
evidence: Developmental dynamics analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a marginal increase in heart rate percentiles during mature contact calls during late development (PND 52-61) compared to early development (PND 1-10).
source: There was a marginal increase in heart rate percentiles during mature contact calls during late development (PND 52–61) as compared to early development (PND 1–10) (Early = 490 calls; Late = 780 calls; β ±SE = 6.28±3.48, t = 1.81, p=0.0795; Appendix 1.10).
evidence: Statistical comparison between early and late developmental periods.

claim: Locomotor activity events occurred when heart rate percentiles were elevated above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test.
source: A summary of the real-time dynamics of heart rate fluctuations in the 10 s before to 10 s after locomotion events revealed that these events occurred when heart rate percentiles were elevated above the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test (Figure 4C).
evidence: Analysis of temporal dynamics with bootstrap significance testing shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Changes in arousal during locomotor activity happened at least 10 seconds before the start of movement.
source: As with vocal production, this change in arousal was 'global', meaning that the change in arousal happened well before (at least 10 s) the start of movement.
evidence: Observation from temporal dynamics analysis of heart rate around locomotor activity.

claim: Heart rate percentiles during locomotor activity continued to increase throughout the first two months of postnatal life.
source: Early in postnatal life, heart rate percentiles during locomotor activity were within the 95% threshold of the bootstrap significance test, but continued to increase throughout the first two months of postnatal life.
evidence: Developmental dynamics analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was a marginal increase in heart rate percentiles during locomotor events during late development (PND 52-61) compared to early development (PND 1-10).
source: There was a marginal increase in heart rate percentiles during locomotor events during late development (PND 52–61) as compared to early development (PND 1–10) (Early = 752 calls; Late = 566 calls; β ±SE = 8.12±4.04, t = 2.01, p=0.0580; Appendix 1.11).
evidence: Statistical comparison between early and late developmental periods.

claim: Locomotor activity during mature contact call production was positively associated with heart rate percentiles.
source: Locomotor activity during mature contact call production was positively associated with heart rate percentiles (n = 3966 calls, β ±SE = 9.66±4.05, t = 2.39, p=0.0208; Appendix 1.12; Figure 5B).
evidence: Statistical analysis using linear mixed model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The positive association between locomotor activity and heart rate percentiles characterized infants that were one month old (1-30 days) but not two months old (31-61 days).
source: Specifically, this positive association characterized infants that were one month old (1–30 days; n = 1705 calls, β ±SE = 16.32±6.60, t = 2.47, Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p=0.0382; Appendix 1.12), but not two months old (31–61 days; n = 2261 calls, β ±SE = 2.63±5.24, t = 0.50, Bonferroni-Holm adjusted p=0.6220; Appendix 1.12).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing different age groups.

claim: Marmoset monkey vocalizations develop sooner than postural-locomotor skills.
source: We found that marmoset monkey vocalizations develop sooner than postural-locomotor skills
evidence: Summary conclusion from developmental trajectory analyses.

claim: Locomotor activity gradually becomes coordinated with the production of mature-sounding contact calls.
source: that locomotor activity gradually becomes coordinated with the production of mature-sounding contact calls
evidence: Summary conclusion from developmental dynamics analyses.

claim: Vocal-locomotor coordination occurs during elevated levels of arousal.
source: and that this vocal-locomotor coordination occurs during elevated levels of arousal.
evidence: Summary conclusion from heart rate and coordination analyses.

claim: Studies investigating real-time coordination between vocal and locomotor outputs show that some vocalizations can be produced concurrently with locomotor activity and/or postural changes, while others cannot.
source: Studies investigating the real-time coordination between vocal and locomotor outputs show that some vocalizations can be produced concurrently with locomotor activity and/or postural changes, while others cannot (Suthers et al., 1972; Blumberg, 1992; Fusani et al., 1996; Williams, 2001; Wong and Waters, 2001; Holderied and von Helversen, 2003; Branchi et al., 2004; Cooper and Goller, 2004; Berg et al., 2013; Dalziell et al., 2013; Hoepfner and Goller, 2013; Ota et al., 2015; Alves et al., 2016; Laplagne and Elías Costa, 2016; Ullrich et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The 'A', 'B' and 'D' song types of the lyrebird (Menura novaehollandiae) co-occur with courtship dance wing flaps, while the 'C' type occurs when wings are still.
source: For example, the 'A', 'B' and 'D' song types of the lyrebird (Menura novaehollandiae) co-occur with courtship dance wing flaps, while the 'C' type occurs when wings are still (Dalziell et al., 2013).
evidence: Example from cited research on lyrebirds.

claim: In rats (Rattus norvegicus), 50 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations are produced during locomotor activity, while 20 kHz vocalizations occur when rats are immobile.
source: In rats (Rattus norvegicus), 50 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations are produced during locomotor activity, while 20 kHz vocalizations occur when rats are immobile (Laplagne and Elías Costa, 2016).
evidence: Example from cited research on rats.

claim: Bats in flight coordinate the production of echolocation sounds with particular phases of their wing beats.
source: Similarly, bats in flight coordinate the production of echolocation sounds with particular phases of their wing beats (Suthers et al., 1972; Wong and Waters, 2001; Holderied and von Helversen, 2003).
evidence: Example from cited research on bats.

claim: There is evidence that locomotor skills at one time point predict speech ability months or even years later in humans.
source: In support of this, there is evidence that locomotor skills at one time point predict speech ability months or even years later (LeBarton and Iverson, 2013; Walle and Campos, 2014; Wang et al., 2014; He et al., 2015; LeBarton and Iverson, 2016; Libertus and Violi, 2016; Walle, 2016; Garrido et al., 2017; Libertus and Hauf, 2017; Salavati et al., 2017; West et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Infant production of pre-linguistic vocalization is highly sensitive to body movement.
source: These studies showed that infant production of pre-linguistic vocalization is highly sensitive to body movement.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited human infant studies.

claim: Infants who are beginning to transverse their environment (i.e., crawling) are less likely to vocalize during locomotion than while they are sitting.
source: For example, infants who are beginning to transverse their environment (i.e., crawling) are less likely to vocalize during locomotion than while they are sitting (Ejiri and Masataka, 2001; Fagan and Iverson, 2007; Abney et al., 2014; Berger et al., 2017).
evidence: Example from cited research on human infants.

claim: Humans exhibit an increase in arousal (as measured by heart rate) prior to speaking.
source: Humans, for example, exhibit an increase in arousal--as measured by heart rate--prior to speaking (Lynch et al., 1980; Linden, 1987).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Infant marmosets spontaneously produce sequences of immature and mature vocalizations that are linked to real-time changes in arousal levels.
source: In the vocal domain, infant marmosets spontaneously produce sequences of immature and mature vocalizations, and these are linked to real-time changes in arousal levels (Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Over approximately two months, infant marmosets exhibit changes in the acoustic properties of their vocalizations that reflect a transition from producing mostly immature-sounding contact calls (e.g., cries) to mature-sounding contact calls (e.g., phees).
source: Over the course of approximately two months, infants exhibit changes in the acoustic properties of their vocalizations that reflect a transition from producing mostly immature-sounding contact calls (e.g., cries) to mature-sounding contact calls (e.g., phees) (Takahashi et al., 2015; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016; Teramoto et al., 2017; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The transition from immature to mature vocalizations in marmosets is facilitated by and dependent upon social reinforcement from parents.
source: As in humans (Goldstein and Ja, 2008), this transition is facilitated by, and dependent upon, social reinforcement from parents (Takahashi et al., 2015; Gultekin and Hage, 2017; Takahashi et al., 2017; Gultekin and Hage, 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Marmoset monkey development transitions from immature to mature forms in a pattern similar to human development.
source: In the postural and locomotor domains, marmoset monkey development transitions from immature to mature forms in a pattern that is also similar to human development (e.g., righting reflex before sitting, and crawling before walking) (Wang et al., 2014; Braun et al., 2015; Schultz-Darken et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Postural-locomotor maturity is not required for vocal development to occur.
source: These results suggest that postural-locomotor maturity is not required for vocal development to occur
evidence: Interpretation of findings from developmental trajectory analyses.

claim: Infants gradually improve coordination between vocalizations and body movement through a process that may be facilitated by arousal level changes.
source: and that infants gradually improve coordination between vocalizations and body movement through a process that may be facilitated by arousal level changes.
evidence: Interpretation of findings with speculative element about mechanism.

claim: Marmoset monkey motor development takes the form of a head-to-tail sequence.
source: Our data suggest that, like humans and other animals (Starck and Ricklefs, 1998; Muir, 2000; Adolph, 2008), marmoset monkey motor development takes the form of a head-to-tail sequence.
evidence: Interpretation of findings compared to established developmental patterns in other species.

claim: An initial investment in the vocal system allows infants to elicit caregiver attention more effectively, thereby prolonging the amount of time they need to develop their locomotor autonomy.
source: One explanation is that an initial investment in the vocal system allows infants to elicit caregiver attention (e.g., carrying and food sharing) more effectively, thereby prolonging the amount of time they need to develop their locomotor autonomy.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed developmental sequence.

claim: More adult-like sounds elicit caregiver attention better than immature sounds in marmosets and humans.
source: Previous work in marmosets and humans suggests that more adult-like sounds elicit caregiver attention better than do immature sounds (Gros-Louis et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A mismatch between biomechanical dynamics of the vocal system is thought to generate immature cries instead of mature contact calls in developing marmosets.
source: In developing marmosets, a mismatch between biomechanical dynamics of the vocal system is thought to generate immature cries instead of mature contact calls (Teramoto et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Vigorous motor activities, like running, speed up breathing cycles.
source: Vigorous motor activities, like running, speed up breathing cycles (Wasserman et al., 1973; Bramble and Carrier, 1983)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Speeding up breathing cycles results in articulation deficits.
source: Vigorous motor activities, like running, speed up breathing cycles (Wasserman et al., 1973; Bramble and Carrier, 1983), resulting in articulation deficits (Sundberg et al., 1991; Price et al., 2006; Baker et al., 2008; Orlikoff, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Calls produced during movement being shorter and noisier indicates that very young marmosets lacked adequate respiratory power.
source: The finding that calls produced during movement were shorter and noisier indicates that very young marmosets lacked adequate respiratory power (Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citation.

claim: Heart rate increases at a faster rate during sustained exercise in adults who are engaged in a speech task than in adults engaged in a non-speech task.
source: For example, heart rate increases at a faster rate during sustained exercise in adults who are engaged in a speech task than in adults engaged in a non-speech task (Baker et al., 2008).
evidence: Example from cited research on humans.

claim: Arousal state is a key player in the coordination between vocal and locomotor systems during development.
source: Our study design precludes testing causality but does suggest that arousal state is a key player in the coordination between vocal and locomotor systems during development.
evidence: Interpretation of findings with acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: Marmosets gradually improved their ability to coordinate locomotor behaviors with vocal production over development.
source: This developmental shift suggests that marmosets gradually improved their ability to coordinate locomotor behaviors with vocal production.
evidence: Interpretation of developmental dynamics findings.

claim: Improvement in vocal-locomotor coordination suggests that marmosets acquired the ability to better control the vocal apparatus during movement.
source: From a biomechanical perspective, this improvement suggests that marmosets acquired the ability to better control the vocal apparatus during movement.
evidence: Speculative interpretation from biomechanical perspective.

claim: Improvement in vocal-locomotor coordination suggests that more experience with vocal behaviors and/or locomotion leads to better coordination between these motor systems.
source: From a neural perspective, this improvement suggests that more experience with vocal behaviors and/or locomotion leads to better coordination between these motor systems.
evidence: Speculative interpretation from neural perspective.

claim: Shifting dynamics of the autonomic nervous system may create the scaffolding by which mature social behavior can emerge.
source: One intriguing possibility is that these shifting dynamics of the autonomic nervous system create the scaffolding by which mature social behavior can emerge (Porges and Furman, 2011).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Infant marmosets require considerable muscular effort to produce mature contact calls (phees).
source: Infant marmosets require considerable muscular effort to produce mature contact calls (phees) (Takahashi et al., 2015; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2016; Zhang and Ghazanfar, 2018)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Adult marmosets tend to produce mature contact calls during periods of reduced locomotor activity.
source: and adult marmosets tend to produce mature contact calls during periods of reduced locomotor activity (Borjon et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Individuals in an elevated arousal state are better able to coordinate mature vocal production with locomotion.
source: In other words, this result suggests that individuals in an elevated arousal state are better able to coordinate mature vocal production with locomotion.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical findings on arousal and vocal-locomotor coordination.

claim: There is a particularly robust relationship between locomotor activity and heart rate during early infanthood when individuals are transitioning from producing immature to mature contact calls.
source: Instead, there may be a particularly robust relationship between locomotor activity and heart rate during early infanthood when individuals are transitioning from producing immature to mature contact calls.
evidence: Interpretation of age-specific statistical findings.

claim: Elevated arousal may help to overcome physiological demands (e.g., respiratory power) of producing vocalizations while moving.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that elevated arousal may help to overcome physiological demands (e.g., respiratory power) of producing vocalizations while moving.
evidence: Interpretation of findings as consistent with a hypothesis.

claim: The subjects were born in captivity and lived with their family groups (mother, father and siblings).
source: Subjects were born in captivity and lived with their family groups (mother, father and siblings).
evidence: Description of subject housing conditions.

claim: The colony room was maintained at a temperature of approximately 27°C with 50-60% relative humidity, and a 12:12 hr light-dark cycle.
source: The colony room was maintained at a temperature of approximately 27° C with 50–60% relative humidity, and a 12:12 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: Description of housing conditions.

claim: All subjects had ad libitum access to water and were supplied daily with standard commercial chow supplemented with fruit and vegetables.
source: All subjects had ad libitum access to water and were supplied daily with standard commercial chow supplemented with fruit and vegetables.
evidence: Description of feeding conditions.

claim: Each observation session lasted 10 minutes.
source: All observation sessions were conducted during daylight hours between postnatal day 1 to 61, and each observation session lasted 10 minutes.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol.

claim: A total of 10,956 calls were recorded across all subjects.
source: We recorded audio for 192 of the 220 observation sessions (Subjects 1–7: 28, 29, 21, 20, 31, 31, 32) for a total of 10,956 calls (Subjects 1–7: 1,100, 801, 1,604, 1,021, 1,657, 2,199, 2,574).
evidence: Description of data collection results.

claim: A total of 3195 instances of specific postural-locomotor behaviors were identified.
source: We recorded video for 215 of the 220 observation sessions and identified a total of 3195 instances of specific postural-locomotor behaviors (Subjects 1–7: 662, 635, 414, 574, 207, 427, 276).
evidence: Description of data collection results.

claim: Heart rate was recorded for 149 of the 220 observation sessions.
source: To quantify arousal fluctuations, we recorded heart rate for 149 of the 220 observation sessions (Subjects 1–7: 16, 14, 21, 19, 26, 25, 28).
evidence: Description of data collection results.

claim: Wiener entropy is a non-positive number calculated by taking the logarithm of the ratio between the geometric and arithmetic means of the values of the power spectrum for different frequencies.
source: Wiener entropy is a non-positive number that is calculated by taking the logarithm of the ratio between the geometric and arithmetic means of the values of the power spectrum for different frequencies (Tchernichovski et al., 2000).
evidence: Definition of acoustic measure with citation.

claim: Wiener entropy represents the broadband properties of a signal's power spectrum in which the closer the signal is to white noise, the higher (closer to zero) the entropy value.
source: Wiener entropy represents the broadband properties of a signal's power spectrum in which the closer the signal is to white noise, the higher (closer to zero) the entropy value.
evidence: Explanation of acoustic measure interpretation.
